title: Has My MTD Update Been Submitted? How to Check the Evidence
excerpt: An uploaded document or completed bookkeeping task is not proof that HMRC has received your MTD update. Check the submission result, the business concerned and the reporting period before treating the job as complete.
metaTitle: Has Your MTD Update Been Submitted? Check the Evidence | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Check your MTD quarterly update submission using HMRC activity and software confirmation. Match the business, tax year and period before treating it as filed.
featuredImageAlt: A taxpayer and accountant compare a software submission result, confirmation document and reporting-period calendar.

sources.label: HMRC / GOV.UK — send quarterly updates
GOV.UK — Personal tax account

content:
Match the HMRC activity and software confirmation to the correct business, tax year and update period. Uploading receipts or finishing bookkeeping is not proof of submission. If the evidence is missing or contradictory, ask the accountant to check before anyone sends a duplicate.

Ask for evidence with four matching details

The confirmation should identify the business or property source, tax year, update period and submission outcome. Keep a reference or receipt where available. If you have a trade and property, proof of one does not establish that both were sent.

Check HMRC activity and software results

HMRC says recent activity in the online account shows a sent update. Compatible software should also show the result. If an accountant files, ask for that confirmation rather than relying only on a progress message.

Understand the period shown

A standard second 2026/27 update covers 6 April to 5 October 2026. A confirmation for a different period or business is not proof of that obligation. Match cumulative coverage, especially after a handover.

If the evidence does not agree

Ask the accountant to check the filing software and HMRC account. A failed submission, a delayed display and an incomplete records task need different responses. Do not send a duplicate simply because a screen has not refreshed.

Retain the figures reviewed, any correction queries and final confirmation together. If something failed, record the error, who will resolve it and when the result will be checked. These records make a later accountant handover easier too.

Check your own HMRC activity

Sign in through the official personal tax account entry point using your own details. HMRC’s guidance says recent activity shows “You sent a quarterly update”. Match the relevant business and period with the software confirmation.

If the software says submitted but the account does not agree, give the accountant both pieces of evidence and ask it to verify the outcome. Do not turn an uncertain display into a second filing. Agree when you will receive the checked result.

Match the receipt to the actual obligation

Illustrative example.

A taxpayer runs a trade and also has a property business. A confirmation for the trade’s first update does not show that the property business’s second update was filed. A green “complete” badge without the business and period is not enough to resolve that question.

Ask the accountant to match each obligation to its submission result and HMRC activity. Keep the date, business, tax year, period and available confirmation together. If one source is missing, agree who investigates it before attempting another submission.

Actions to take
CheckPractical action
BusinessMatch the correct trade or property business.
PeriodCheck the tax year and cumulative coverage dates.
OutcomeCheck actual submission evidence rather than document-upload status.

Does a successful bank feed prove submission?

No. Imported transactions are an input to record-keeping, not filing evidence.

Should I submit again if the dashboard is slow?

Check the software outcome and HMRC activity first. Resolve the uncertainty before attempting another filing.

excerpt: If HMRC has signed you up for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax, here is what that means, the practical steps to take next, and how an accountant-led service can help.

GOV.UK — Find out if and when you need to use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
GOV.UK — Use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax

content:
Check the HMRC notice, confirm your business and property income sources and arrange compatible software or an authorised accountant. If HMRC has signed you up for 2026/27, organise digital records from the tax-year start and check which updates remain outstanding. Your earlier Self Assessment return can still be due.

Confirm what HMRC has done

HMRC began signing up people in the 2026/27 cohort who had not signed up themselves. That generally concerns qualifying income over £50,000 in 2024/25. Check the genuine HMRC notice and your online account instead of assuming any message about MTD is authentic.

Check the income sources it holds

HMRC uses information it already has. Confirm which trades and property sources continue, which have stopped and whether a new source is missing. Use the actual start or cessation dates. If you believe you should not be in scope or are exempt, contact HMRC with the relevant evidence.

Choose how the records and filings will be handled

You need suitable software, either used yourself or through an authorised accountant. Bring the digital records up to date from the tax-year start. Check which cumulative updates have been sent and keep the confirmations. A signup notice alone does not show those updates are complete.

First-year relief does not remove the work

HMRC is not applying quarterly-update penalty points for 2026/27, but records and updates are still required. Late annual returns and late tax payments have their own consequences. Your 2025/26 Self Assessment return can also remain due on 31 January 2027.

If you want TaxSimba to help

Send the notice, income-source details and existing filing evidence when enquiring about MTD support. Confirm the work and period included before purchase. Use the incorrect-signup guide if the issue is whether HMRC should have put you in MTD at all.

A useful order for your first checks

  1. Read the notice and check the signup in your HMRC account.
  2. List the continuing businesses and records already held.
  3. Check software and agent arrangements, including who can file.
  4. Identify outstanding updates and agree the catch-up work.
  5. Keep the earlier Self Assessment return on its own task list.

Bring those five answers to an enquiry. They help distinguish a straightforward setup from missing-records work. If the notice looks wrong, use the guide to disputing MTD signup rather than buying a service on the assumption that the notice must be correct.

Use the notice to check the underlying records

Illustrative example.

A fictional sole trader stopped one activity but still receives rental income. They should not assume that ceasing the trade means every MTD obligation has ended. Check which sources remain and what dates HMRC holds.

A different taxpayer whose trading and property sources all ceased needs the cessation dates checked against HMRC’s guidance. Keeping the notice, the source list and the dates together is more useful than treating “signed up” as a complete description of their circumstances. Do not discard the earlier Self Assessment return task while setting up current-year records.

Actions to take
CheckPractical action
Income-source recordIdentify continuing, new and ceased sources and the actual dates.
Software or agentConfirm coverage and responsibility for the remaining obligations.
Earlier-year returnCheck it separately from current-year MTD setup.

Do I have to wait for another HMRC letter?

Use the official HMRC service to check your position and follow the applicable guidance. Do not leave a confirmed obligation unattended while waiting for a repeat notice.

Does first-year penalty relief remove the record-keeping requirement?

No. The relief for quarterly-update penalty points does not mean digital records and required updates can be abandoned.

  • Continuing, new and ceased income sources
  • Actual cessation dates where relevant
  • Software, agent and outstanding-update plan
  • Earlier-year annual-return status

title: MTD Qualifying Income Explained — Does the £50,000 Rule Apply to Me?
excerpt: Qualifying income is the figure HMRC uses to decide when Making Tax Digital for Income Tax applies. Here is what counts, what does not, and how the £50,000 threshold fits in.
metaTitle: MTD Qualifying Income: Which Income Counts? | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Check MTD qualifying income using gross self-employment and property income. Separate PAYE and other income, then match the correct tax year and threshold.
featuredImageAlt: An independent trader separates gross business invoices and rental statements from a payslip; three distinct piles and a magnifying glass.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Work out your qualifying income for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
GOV.UK — Find out if and when you need to use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax

content:
MTD qualifying income is the relevant gross self-employment and property income before expenses. Combine the sources and use the correct lookback year. PAYE salary does not count towards this total, and profit after expenses is not the threshold figure.

What counts as qualifying income

HMRC adds up income from:

  • self-employment
  • property (including, where relevant, more than one source)

That total can come from several trades or properties. It is based on the Self Assessment return HMRC uses to assess the relevant year, not on a rough guess from your bank balance.

What usually does not count

These are generally not part of qualifying income for MTD threshold checks:

  • employment income taxed through PAYE
  • State Pension and private pensions
  • dividends (including from your own company)
  • your share of profit as an individual partner in a partnership (with limited exceptions explained on GOV.UK)

You may still need Self Assessment for those incomes. They just do not drive the MTD qualifying-income total in the same way.

How the £50,000 rule fits the timeline

According to current GOV.UK guidance, if your qualifying income is over:

  • £50,000 for 2024 to 2025: MTD from 6 April 2026
  • £30,000 for 2025 to 2026: MTD from 6 April 2027
  • £20,000 for 2026 to 2027: MTD from 6 April 2028

HMRC reviews returns and may write to you. Even without a letter, it is still your responsibility to check whether you need to use MTD.

Example

Jordan has £27,000 rental turnover and £26,000 self-employment turnover in the same tax year. Qualifying income is £53,000 before expenses. That is over £50,000, so the April 2026 MTD start can apply even though neither figure alone looks “huge.”

Common mistake

Using profit after expenses, or adding PAYE salary into the total, then deciding you are “safely under £50,000.” Threshold checks are based on HMRC’s qualifying-income rules. Read the official GOV.UK page rather than social media shortcuts.

What to do next

  1. Work out your self-employment and property totals using GOV.UK’s qualifying-income guidance.
  2. Use HMRC’s checker and TaxSimba’s MTD checker as a practical prompt, then confirm against official rules.
  3. If you are in scope (or already signed up), plan digital records and quarterly updates.
  4. Decide whether you want accountant-led support via the Making Tax Digital service.

Check the year before adding the income

Illustrative preparation example.

Your latest trade receipts are £22,000, but the HMRC notice uses an earlier return. Put each year’s trade and property income on a separate line before comparing a threshold. Mixing this year’s trade receipts with last year’s rent creates a total that belongs to neither year.

Check: Which completed return and income sources support the start date in your notice?

Actions to take
CheckPractical action
Sole-trade turnoverUse the relevant gross business income before expenses.
Property incomeInclude the relevant property income and ownership share.
Assessment yearMatch the total to the correct phase and official threshold.

Does a low profit put me outside MTD?

Not by itself: turnover and profit are different figures. Check the qualifying-income calculation before relying on expenses.

Should I use the latest bank balance?

No. Use records for the tax year HMRC assesses, distinguishing income from transfers and other receipts.

  • Gross income from each sole trade
  • Property income and ownership shares
  • PAYE and other excluded income kept separate

title: MTD Quarterly Updates — What Do I Actually Need to Send?
excerpt: Quarterly updates are summaries of your self-employment and property income and expenses — not a full tax return. Here is what goes to HMRC and when.
metaTitle: MTD Quarterly Updates: Records, Totals and Evidence | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Understand what MTD quarterly updates contain, how cumulative periods work and what evidence to keep after compatible software sends the summary.
featuredImageAlt: An electrician and accountant transform many invoices into a tidy single summary ledger, with a calendar nearby.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax - Send quarterly updates - Guidance
GOV.UK — Use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax - Create digital records - Guidance
GOV.UK — Use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax - Guidance

content:
Send cumulative income and expense category totals from your digital records through MTD-compatible software, or have your agent send them. It is not a full annual tax return or a folder of invoices. Keep the correct business, period and submission confirmation together.

What actually gets sent

Your software adds up digital records for each business and produces totals using the same broad income and expense categories used in Self Assessment. Each quarterly update covers from the start of the tax year to the end of that update period, so it shows year-to-date totals. If you need to correct something, update your digital records in the software so later updates reflect the right figures, following HMRC’s process.

You do not need to make accounting or tax adjustments before sending a quarterly update. If you had no income or expenses in a period, you still need to send the update.

When they are due (standard update periods)

If your accounting period aligns with the tax year (6 April to 5 April), GOV.UK sets out standard periods and deadlines including:

  • 6 April to 5 July: send by 7 August
  • 6 April to 5 October: send by 7 November
  • 6 April to 5 January: send by 7 February
  • 6 April to 5 April: send by 7 May (following tax year)

Calendar update periods exist for some 1 April–31 March accounting periods. The send-by deadlines above stay the same. Your software should show the dates that apply to you.

Example

Riley is a self-employed electrician in MTD. Throughout the year Riley stores invoices and expenses digitally. Before each deadline, compatible software (used with accountant oversight through TaxSimba) produces the quarterly totals for Riley to check, then sends the update. Riley is not emailing HMRC a folder of PDF receipts every quarter.

Common mistake

Treating quarterlies as optional “practice runs” before Self Assessment. For people in MTD, quarterly updates are required. For 2026 to 2027, HMRC will not apply penalty points for late quarterly updates, but you still need to send them before you can submit your tax return, and late-return penalties can still apply.

What to do next

  1. Confirm you are in MTD (or have been signed up).
  2. Keep digital records as you go, not in a January shoebox.
  3. Diary the quarterly deadlines your software shows.
  4. Decide whether an accountant or agent should send updates for you. If you want managed help, see the Making Tax Digital service.

Reconcile a category before approving the update

Illustrative preparation example.

Your software shows £900 of repairs, but the folder contains a £300 invoice entered twice. Reconcile the entries to evidence before approving the cumulative category totals. A complete folder of images cannot show whether a single invoice has been counted twice.

Check: Can you trace the total back to distinct transactions for the correct business and period?

Actions to take
CheckPractical action
Input recordsReconcile the transactions and preserve supporting evidence.
Update periodCheck cumulative dates and the correct business.
Submission resultSave confirmation and resolve any error or mismatch.

Does HMRC receive every receipt image?

The quarterly update sends summary totals rather than each invoice. Keep the underlying evidence as part of your records.

Can I skip an update during a quiet period?

Do not assume no activity removes the obligation. Check and send the required update even where the period has no income or expenses.

  • Business and accounting-period setting
  • Income and expense categories reconciled
  • Cumulative period covered
  • Outstanding records or queries
  • Submission outcome and next deadline

title: Self Assessment Deadline 2027 — Dates You Need to Know
excerpt: For the 2025 to 2026 tax year, the online Self Assessment deadline is 31 January 2027. Here are the key dates, what happens if you are late, and how to prepare.
metaTitle: Self Assessment Deadline 2027: Filing and Payment | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Prepare for the 2025/26 Self Assessment deadlines. Distinguish online filing, payment, paper returns and the earlier PAYE collection cutoff.
featuredImageAlt: A freelancer plans filing and payment on separate calendar notes while gathering documents early at an oak desk.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Self Assessment tax returns: Deadlines
GOV.UK — Self Assessment tax returns: Overview
GOV.UK — Understand your Self Assessment tax bill: Payments on account

content:
For 2025/26, the usual online Self Assessment filing and payment deadline is 31 January 2027. Paper returns are normally due on 31 October 2026. PAYE collection requests have an earlier online deadline, and a specific HMRC notice can change the filing date.

Key dates for the 2027 filing season

  • 31 October 2026: paper tax return deadline (if you still file on paper).
  • 30 December 2026: online deadline if you want HMRC to collect through your tax code where that option applies.
  • 31 January 2027: online return and payment deadline for most people.
  • 31 July: second payment on account deadline where payments on account apply.

If you need to tell HMRC you should be in Self Assessment for the first time (or again after a gap), GOV.UK also sets a 5 October registration-related deadline for the previous tax year. Check the deadlines page for the exact wording that applies to you, and see our 5 October registration guide.

What “deadline” covers

People often hear “31 January” and only think about clicking submit. In practice you usually need:

  • the return filed online, and
  • the balancing payment paid on time

Filing on time but paying late can still create charges. Payments on account, if they apply, are a separate rhythm. They are not a surprise “extra bill” invented by your accountant. See payments on account explained.

Example

Priya freelances and also has a small rental. She gathers records in autumn, uses TaxSimba’s accountant-led Self Assessment service to prepare the return, reviews it in December, and files well before 31 January 2027 instead of discovering missing invoices in the last week of January.

Common mistake

Waiting for a perfect final bank export on 30 January. If something is missing, you still need a plan: file on time with best available figures only where HMRC rules allow, or get advice quickly. Do not simply ghost the deadline.

If you later spot a genuine mistake on a return you already filed, that is usually an amendment problem, not a second “deadline” — act within HMRC’s correction window.

Getting ready

  1. Confirm which tax year you are filing for and diary 31 January 2027.
  2. Build a document checklist (income, expenses, property, dividends, and so on). See the documents checklist.
  3. Start early if your affairs are mixed or you may also have MTD obligations.
  4. Choose DIY software carefully, or use the Self Assessment accountant service if you want preparation handled.

Give filing and payment their own completion dates

Illustrative preparation example.

You approve a return on 20 January, but have no submission confirmation and have not arranged payment. Keep approval, filing and payment as three separate lines. Each needs its own evidence; marking the email approved does not finish the other two.

Check: Which of the three tasks is complete, and who is responsible for the remaining ones?

Actions to take
CheckPractical action
Return filingCheck the tax year, route and applicable deadline.
PaymentCheck the bill and allow time for the chosen payment method.
Special noticeRetain and read any HMRC deadline letter separately.

Does filing early mean paying immediately?

Filing and payment dates are separate. Check the actual amount and due date rather than assuming the submission date creates a new deadline.

What if a supplier document is missing?

Identify the gap early and ask how HMRC's rules apply. Missing evidence is not a reason to invent figures or ignore the deadline.

  • Tax year and filing route
  • Applicable HMRC notice
  • Return preparation and approval status
  • Tax and payments-on-account amounts
  • Payment method and confirmation

title: What Documents Do I Need for My Self Assessment Tax Return?
excerpt: A practical Self Assessment document checklist for sole traders, landlords and people with mixed income — so you are not hunting for paperwork in January.
metaTitle: Self Assessment Documents: Build a Complete Record Pack | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Gather Self Assessment documents by income source: PAYE, business, property, savings, investments and other relevant records. Identify gaps before filing.
featuredImageAlt: A mixed-income worker places payslips, rental records, invoices and savings certificates into clearly distinct folders.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Self Assessment tax returns: Overview
GOV.UK — Business records if you're self-employed: Overview
GOV.UK — Expenses if you're self-employed: Overview
GOV.UK — Work out your rental income when you let property

content:
Gather your HMRC references, income statements, business or rental records, expense evidence and details of relevant pensions, donations, gains and loans. Use the tax year the return covers. Tell the accountant what is missing rather than waiting for a perfect folder.

Core documents most people should gather

  • National Insurance number and Unique Taxpayer Reference (UTR) if you have one
  • P60 / P45 / P11D where you also had employment
  • Bank statements covering the tax year
  • Records of other untaxed income you must report

If you are self-employed or freelancing

  • Sales invoices and payment records (turnover)
  • Expense receipts and bills that are wholly and exclusively for business
  • Mileage or travel logs if you claim them
  • Home-as-office workings if relevant
  • Details of any stock, equipment or capital purchases

HMRC expects you to keep business records. Digital copies are fine if they are clear and complete.

If you have rental income

  • Rent received (statements from agents help)
  • Allowable property expenses (repairs, insurance, agent fees, and similar)
  • Mortgage interest information where it affects your property calculations
  • Dates properties were let, empty or personally used

Other common extras

  • Dividend vouchers or broker summaries
  • Bank / building society interest certificates
  • Capital gains information if you disposed of assets
  • Pension contribution records
  • Charitable donation evidence for Gift Aid
  • Student loan plan details if repayments interact with your return

Example

Alex freelances and lets one flat. Before using TaxSimba, Alex exports business bank CSV files, saves PDF invoices, downloads the letting agent’s annual statement, and photographs repair receipts. The accountant can prepare the return from that pack instead of chasing missing items in January.

Common mistake

Keeping only the “big” invoices and losing small recurring costs (software, phone, insurance). Those small items add up, and without evidence they are hard to support if HMRC asks questions.

If you already filed and then find missing documents that change the figures, use HMRC’s amendment process rather than hoping the gap never matters.

Build your pack

  1. List your income types for the tax year.
  2. Create a simple folder (digital is fine) per category.
  3. Note gaps early. Do not discover them on 30 January.
  4. If you want help, start the Self Assessment service and upload as you go.

Mark a missing document with an owner

Illustrative preparation example.

A P60 is ready, one rental statement is missing and the savings account has not been checked. Send the available records with a short gap list. Name who will obtain each missing item and when, instead of sending a folder that appears complete.

Check: Does your cover sheet identify missing records across every income source?

Actions to take
CheckPractical action
Income-source listList every relevant source before sorting documents.
Period coverageCheck start and end dates on each statement.
Missing evidenceRecord who will obtain it and by when.

Do bank statements explain every payment?

Not always. Keep invoices, statements and explanations for transfers, private spending and unusual transactions.

Should I send only documents showing income?

Include relevant expense, tax-deducted and other evidence as well. The exact pack depends on your circumstances.

  • Income sources for the tax year
  • PAYE and tax-deducted documents
  • Business or property supporting evidence
  • Statement coverage and missing records
  • Named owner and date for each gap

title: A Simple Guide to UK Self Assessment
excerpt: Self Assessment is how HMRC collects Income Tax from people who need to report income themselves each year — including many self-employed people and landlords.
metaTitle: UK Self Assessment: Who Files and What Happens | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Understand UK Self Assessment, when to check whether a return is needed, what records to prepare and how filing differs from paying the bill.
featuredImageAlt: A first-time taxpayer and accountant open an organised return folder together, simple welcoming introductory scene.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Self Assessment tax returns: Overview
GOV.UK — Who must send a tax return
GOV.UK — Self Assessment deadlines

content:
Self Assessment is how you report income and gains that need an individual tax return. A PAYE job does not settle every other income source. Check whether a return is required, gather the records for the correct tax year and file and pay by the applicable deadlines.

Check whether you need a return

For 2025/26, a sole trader with gross income over £1,000 generally needs to file. Other triggers include partnership membership, relevant gains and certain untaxed income or charges. PAYE salary alone is not a universal filing trigger. Use HMRC’s return checker, and do not ignore a notice to file while you seek clarification.

Know which year you are reporting

The 2025/26 tax year ran from 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026. The usual online filing and payment deadline is 31 January 2027; paper filing is normally due by 31 October 2026. A specific HMRC notice can set a different filing date. If you need to register or reactivate after 5 October, follow the instructions in that notice and keep the tax payment deadline separate.

Build the figures from evidence

Collect PAYE documents, trade or rental records, interest and dividend statements, pension and donation details, gains and any loan-repayment information. Different income sources belong in the same personal return where required. Bank transfers between your own accounts are not fresh earnings.

A return and a payment are different steps

Review the complete return before it is filed, then keep the submission confirmation. Check the tax calculation and HMRC account for what remains payable. PAYE or CIS already deducted can affect the balance; payments on account can add advance payments for the following year.

If MTD applies as well

MTD changes how in-scope business and property income is recorded and reported. It does not wipe out an earlier return. Keep 2025/26 Self Assessment and 2026/27 MTD work on separate timelines.

Use the document checklist to prepare. If you want accountant-led help, compare TaxSimba’s current packages and describe all income sources before buying.

You discover that your side business may need reporting. First check the filing requirement, then confirm registration, gather the correct year’s figures, review the draft, obtain filing evidence and arrange any payment. Put these tasks on a timeline so registration is not mistaken for a finished return.

title: Six Tax-Saving Checks for UK Sole Traders
excerpt: Practical ways sole traders and small businesses can stay compliant while claiming what they are entitled to — without aggressive tax schemes.
metaTitle: Sole Trader Tax Savings: Six Practical Checks | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Review expenses, the trading allowance, PAYE and CIS credits, pensions and payments on account. Six practical checks for a sole trader tax return.
featuredImageAlt: A small-business owner compares receipts with expenses and separates a personal shopping bag from business supplies.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Expenses if you're self-employed: Overview
GOV.UK — Tax-free allowances on property and trading income

content:
For a sole trader, useful tax-saving checks include allowable expenses, the choice between expenses and the trading allowance, pension relief and tax already deducted. Each depends on your circumstances. A deduction reduces taxable profit; it does not make a purchase free.

1. Claim genuine costs you can support

For a sole trader, allowable business expenses reduce taxable profit. Keep invoices and explain any private use. Business software, insurance and qualifying travel are worth checking; ordinary clothing, personal spending and fines do not become deductible because they passed through a business account.

Spending £100 to get a deduction does not save £100 of tax. The benefit depends on the tax treatment and your circumstances. Buy what the business needs rather than spending solely to reduce a bill.

2. Compare the trading allowance with actual expenses

Where eligible, the £1,000 trading allowance is an alternative to deducting actual expenses. You do not normally claim both for the same trade. If genuine costs exceed the allowance, using the allowance without comparing can be worse. Exclusions and several trades need checking.

3. Keep tax already deducted in the calculation

Provide PAYE documents and CIS statements. Deductions already paid towards the liability should not be omitted or entered as ordinary business costs. A refund depends on the full calculation; it is not a guaranteed reward for filing.

4. Review home-working and vehicle methods

Simplified expenses can reduce record-calculation work where eligible. Compare the permitted alternative to actual costs and do not double claim. Keep vehicle history and business-mile records; one year’s apparently better result does not automatically permit a method change.

5. Tell the accountant about pensions and donations

Pension relief depends on how the contribution was made and the relevant limits. Gift Aid can also affect a personal calculation. Provide statements showing actual payments and any tax relief already applied so the same amount is not relieved twice.

6. Review payments on account when income falls

A supported reduction can improve cash flow, but it does not change the eventual tax liability. Reducing too far can lead to interest. Keep the estimate and update it if trading improves.

This guide concerns sole traders, not a complete company-tax strategy. See the trading allowance, home working and payments on account for the detailed checks. Ask TaxSimba to review the relevant information within the agreed service; savings depend on the facts.

Ask whether spending improves your finances

Illustrative preparation example.

A £500 purchase is not a £500 tax saving. Before buying, ask whether the business needs it, whether relief is available and which year it affects. Review costs already incurred before creating new spending purely to obtain a deduction.

Check: Would the purchase still be worthwhile after paying its cost and allowing for any actual relief?

Private useIdentify any personal element rather than claiming everything.

Can I claim a cost just because the business account paid it?

The payment account alone does not determine deductibility. The purpose and tax treatment still need checking.

Are guaranteed tax-saving promises reliable?

A provider cannot establish your entitlement without the facts. Ask which specific rule and evidence support a proposed claim.

title: Making Tax Digital (MTD): What You Need to Know
excerpt: Making Tax Digital for Income Tax changes how many sole traders and landlords keep records and report to HMRC. Here is the plain-English version.
metaTitle: Making Tax Digital for Income Tax: Practical Overview | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Understand MTD for Income Tax: qualifying income, digital records, quarterly updates and the annual return. Check the rules for your actual start year.
featuredImageAlt: A landlord and trader explore a laptop ledger and four calendar markers with a professional adviser.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax - Guidance
GOV.UK — Find out if and when you need to use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
GOV.UK — MTD quarterly updates

content:
MTD for Income Tax means digital records, quarterly updates and an annual return through compatible software. It applies in phases based on relevant gross self-employment and property income. It changes the reporting process; quarterly updates do not automatically mean quarterly tax payments.

Who starts when?

MTD Income Tax phases and lookback years
Relevant qualifying incomeIncome year usedStart date
Over £50,0002024/256 April 2026
Over £30,0002025/266 April 2027
Over £20,0002026/276 April 2028

Qualifying income is the relevant gross self-employment and property income before expenses, combined across the relevant sources. PAYE salary is not added to that threshold total. Check exemptions and special circumstances through HMRC rather than deciding from a bank balance.

What changes in practice?

You or your agent keep digital transaction records in a suitable system. Compatible software sends cumulative income and expense category totals to HMRC. After year-end you finalise the annual tax position and submit the return through compatible software. HMRC does not receive every invoice in a quarterly update.

Standard update dates

The standard periods run cumulatively from 6 April to 5 July, 5 October, 5 January and 5 April. The respective deadlines are 7 August, 7 November, 7 February and 7 May. Calendar periods have different coverage dates but the same deadlines. Select the correct basis before the first update is submitted.

What stays separate?

Quarterly reporting does not automatically introduce quarterly tax bills. Service fees, tax payments and payments on account are different. An earlier Self Assessment return can still be due: the usual 2025/26 online deadline is 31 January 2027, while the 2026/27 MTD annual return is due by 31 January 2028.

If you are behind

HMRC’s 2026/27 quarterly penalty-point relief does not make updates optional. Check signup status, outstanding updates and the digital records from the start of the year. Do not ignore the earlier annual return.

Start with qualifying income if eligibility is unclear. For the reporting task, use the update guide. If you prefer managed support, compare TaxSimba’s MTD packages and agree who keeps, checks and submits the records.

Separate setup from ongoing work

Illustrative preparation example.

A software subscription is active, but records are incomplete and no one has accepted the next filing. List signup, software authorisation, digital records, quarterly submissions and annual completion separately. That makes it easier to see whether the problem is access, bookkeeping or responsibility.

Check: Which part is ready, and which still has no named person responsible?

Records and updatesAgree a compatible workflow and reporting responsibilities.
Annual positionPlan the return and actual tax payment separately.

Is MTD for VAT the same service?

No. The taxes, scope and reporting requirements differ. Do not assume an existing VAT setup covers Income Tax.

An appropriately authorised agent can undertake agreed work using compatible software. Confirm the role and service scope.

title: Can an Accountant Handle Making Tax Digital for Me?
excerpt: Yes — you can appoint an accountant or agent for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax. Here is what they can do, what you still need to provide, and how an accountant-led service differs from DIY software.
metaTitle: Can an Accountant Manage MTD? Tasks and Responsibilities | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Check what an MTD accountant or agent can do, which permissions are needed and what records and answers you still need to provide.
featuredImageAlt: An authorised accountant handles a client's organised records while the client supplies missing invoices.

relatedPages.label: Check if MTD applies to you

sources.label: GOV.UK — Use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax - Guidance
GOV.UK — Sign up your client for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
GOV.UK — Choose the right software for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
GOV.UK — Use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax - Create digital records - Guidance

content:
Yes. An authorised accountant can handle agreed MTD work using compatible software. Confirm who keeps the books, sends each update and submits the annual return. You still need to provide complete information and answer questions about it.

Appointing help does not hand HMRC responsibility to someone else in the abstract. You still need to supply complete, accurate information. The accountant manages process and software. They cannot invent missing invoices or guess rent you never recorded.

What an authorised agent can typically help with

In practice, once you have authorised an agent for MTD (and they have the right HMRC agent services setup), they can usually help with:

  • signing you up for MTD where that step is still needed
  • choosing and connecting compatible software
  • creating and maintaining digital records from the evidence you provide
  • preparing and sending quarterly updates
  • helping you complete and submit the year-end tax return through that software

Exact permissions depend on how you authorise them. Ask your accountant to spell out what they will do and what stays with you.

Checklist: what you normally still need to do

  1. Authorise the agent for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax (and Self Assessment where relevant) through HMRC’s agent processes.
  2. Confirm your income sources (self-employment, UK or foreign property, or both) so the right records and updates are set up.
  3. Hand over usable evidence on a steady rhythm: bank exports, sales invoices, expense receipts, letting-agent statements, and notes for anything unusual.
  4. Answer clarifying questions when a transaction is unclear (private vs business, which property, which category).
  5. Review and approve work where your service process asks you to, before updates or the return go to HMRC.
  6. Keep supporting documents. MTD digital records sit alongside the invoices and statements you still need for Self Assessment evidence.

Late or incomplete records make quarterly updates harder for everyone involved. That is a customer-side constraint, not something software can paper over.

DIY software vs accountant support

With DIY-compatible software you drive categorisation, submissions, and HMRC screens yourself. With an accountant-led service such as TaxSimba, you feed information through a client workflow and accountants use compatible software to help manage MTD. TaxSimba is not standalone DIY filing software you are expected to run unsupervised.

DIY can still suit simple affairs if you are comfortable with software and will update records weekly. Mixed income, several properties, or a sudden HMRC signup are usually when people want help.

If you are still checking whether MTD applies

Use GOV.UK’s eligibility guidance and our free MTD checker, then read how qualifying income thresholds work if the £50,000 (and later) figures are unclear.

Prefer not to learn every MTD screen? Compare packages on MTD information and pricing, then start from the Making Tax Digital accountant service if you want managed support rather than DIY software alone. Authorisation and software choices should still follow current GOV.UK guidance for your situation.

Use an unanswered transaction to test responsibility

Illustrative preparation example.

Your bank feed contains a £450 transfer with no explanation. The accountant cannot reliably classify it from the amount alone. Agree how you will answer record queries and when, even where the accountant handles every software submission.

Check: Who answers a transaction query, and what happens if the answer is missing near a deadline?

Agent authorityMatch the authorised role to the agreed tasks.

You still need to provide accurate, complete information and check the return information as required.

Does every supporting agent handle the annual return?

No. Check main-agent responsibilities and who is engaged to finalise and submit the annual return.

title: MTD Digital Records — What You Actually Need to Keep
excerpt: MTD for Income Tax requires digital records of self-employment and property income and expenses. Here is what that means day to day — without the jargon.
metaTitle: MTD Digital Records: Evidence, Categories and Links | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Keep useful MTD digital records with dates, amounts and categories. Preserve receipts and check digital links where records move between software products.
featuredImageAlt: A trader records a receipt on a laptop beside the original paper evidence, showing date and amount as abstract lines.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax - Create digital records - Guidance
GOV.UK — Choose the right software for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
GOV.UK — Use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax - Send quarterly updates - Guidance

content:
Keep digital entries showing the amount, relevant date and category for the business or property transactions in scope, supported by the underlying evidence. A receipt image or bank feed can help, but neither proves the books are complete. Check any simplified-recording rules that apply.

Paper shoeboxes and a January tidy-up are not the design. You should still keep underlying evidence (invoices, statements, receipts). MTD does not mean “delete everything except software totals.”

What each digital record needs

When you create a record, GOV.UK expects at least:

  • amount
  • date the income was received or the expense incurred
  • category, using the same broad Self Assessment-style categories your software supports

Day to day that usually means a clear trail for money in (sales, fees, rent and other taxable income in scope) and money out (allowable expenses), recorded close enough to the transaction that period totals are not guesswork.

For example, a landlord’s boiler repair might be recorded as amount £240, date 12 June 2026, category something like repairs and maintenance (wording depends on the software). The invoice PDF still sits in your files as supporting evidence.

Self-employment and property: different shapes

If you have more than one sole-trader business, GOV.UK expects separate digital records (and separate quarterly updates) for each. UK rental properties are different: they are generally treated as one UK property business, so you do not create a separate MTD “set” per flat. Your software rolls UK property income and expenses into that one business, including your share of jointly let UK property.

Foreign property has its own rules, including separate digital records per foreign property in many cases, even though they still form one foreign property business for the update. Check GOV.UK if you have mixed UK and overseas lets.

One product or several, and digital links

You can use one all-in-one product for records and submissions, or more than one product. If you use more than one, GOV.UK requires them to be digitally linked before you send updates or the return.

Legitimate digital links include methods such as:

  • linked cells or formulas in spreadsheets
  • importing or exporting files (for example CSV or XML) between compatible tools
  • emailing a spreadsheet of digital records for import into another product
  • transferring files on a portable device for import
  • automated data transfer or an API connection

What is not treated as a digital link is manually rewriting figures, or cutting and pasting records between systems after they have been created. Once a digital record has gone to HMRC in a quarterly update, you must not manually move that record around inside or between products in those non-compliant ways. If multi-product linking sounds fiddly, many people prefer an accountant or agent to design the workflow.

When to start

Start from the beginning of the relevant tax year for your accounting period (often 6 April for standard periods, or 1 April if you use calendar update periods). If you join part-way through the year, you may need to catch up records from the start of the year so the first update is complete. Create records as close to each transaction as you reasonably can.

A common mistake

Mixing personal and business spending in one account with no labels, then expecting software or an accountant to reconstruct everything from vague bank descriptions. Cleaner habits through the year make the records usable. For how those records later roll into HMRC summaries, see what quarterly updates contain.

On TaxSimba’s MTD service, you still provide documents and answers. Accountants help organise the compatible-software workflow so records stay usable. Unsure whether MTD applies at all? Confirm on GOV.UK and use the MTD checker as a prompt.

Link the invoice to a usable entry

Choose one supplier invoice. Find the digital entry, check its date, amount and category, then find the supporting document again. If the entry is duplicated or cannot be traced, fix the record rather than adding another copy of the image.

title: I Missed an MTD Quarterly Update — What Should I Do Now?
excerpt: Already past an MTD quarterly deadline? Here is how to catch up, what HMRC’s 2026 to 2027 soft landing means, and when penalty points can apply in later years.
metaTitle: Missed an MTD Update? Catch-Up Steps and Evidence | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Missed an MTD quarterly update? Identify the business and period, repair the records and check submission evidence. Confirm the rules for the relevant year.
featuredImageAlt: A worried trader calmly rebuilds missing records with an accountant and calendar rather than hiding an overdue notice.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax - Send quarterly updates - Guidance
GOV.UK — Penalties for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
GOV.UK — Use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax - Create digital records - Guidance

content:
Bring the records up to date and arrange the overdue update promptly. For 2026/27, HMRC does not apply penalty points for late quarterly updates, but the updates are still required. Annual-return deadlines and tax payments are separate obligations.

For how quarterly updates work when you are on track, use the separate guide on what quarterly updates include and when they are due. This page is only about being late.

Does missing a deadline mean an automatic fine?

For the 2026 to 2027 tax year, HMRC will not apply penalty points for late quarterly updates. That soft landing does not make updates optional. You still need to keep digital records and send the quarterly updates, including before you can submit your tax return. Late tax returns and late payment of tax can still attract penalties.

After 2026 to 2027, late quarterly updates sit in HMRC’s points-based late submission system. In outline: each missed quarterly deadline (and, separately, a missed tax return deadline) can attract a penalty point; the threshold is 4 points; reaching it brings a £200 penalty, and further missed deadlines while at the threshold can each bring another £200. You only get one point per deadline, even if you have more than one business. Always re-check the current GOV.UK MTD penalties page for the year you are in.

Catch-up sequence that usually works

  1. Name the gap: which update period is overdue, and for which self-employment or property business?
  2. Rebuild the digital records from the start of the tax year where catch-up is required (invoices, bank exports, rental statements). Guessing totals to clear a screen is a bad trade.
  3. Send the overdue update through compatible software, or ask your accountant/agent to send it.
  4. Confirm it landed in the software / HMRC view your agent uses, then diary the next deadline your software shows (often 7 August, 7 November, 7 February, 7 May when periods align with the tax year).
  5. Fix the habit that caused the miss: monthly record uploads, calendar reminders, or handing the workflow to an agent.

What not to do

  • Assume the 2026 to 2027 quarterly soft landing means you can skip updates
  • Wait for Self Assessment season and hope the gap disappears
  • Invent figures without evidence just to get past a screen

If you want help getting back on track, TaxSimba’s Making Tax Digital service is set up for people who need records organised and quarterly reporting moving again. You still supply the underlying information. Also useful while you catch up: what digital records to keep and how an accountant can handle MTD.

Rules change by tax year. Confirm deadlines and penalties on GOV.UK before you rely on any summary, including this one.

Turn an overdue screen into a dated plan

Illustrative preparation example.

Two businesses show outstanding work, but records are ready for only one. List the obligations separately, identify each missing period and agree a catch-up date with the filer. Keep the eventual submission confirmations so an overdue label is resolved with evidence.

Check: Which business, period and missing records prevent the next submission?

Actions to take
CheckPractical action
Identify the gapConfirm the business, tax year and reporting period.
Repair and sendResolve missing records and agree who submits.

Should I guess a total to clear the overdue screen?

title: Payments on Account Explained — Why Is HMRC Asking for More?
excerpt: Payments on account are advance payments towards next year’s Self Assessment bill. Here is why HMRC asks for them, when they are due, and when they might not apply.
metaTitle: Payments on Account: January and July Explained | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Understand Self Assessment payments on account, the January balancing payment and how to check your HMRC statement before reducing an instalment.
featuredImageAlt: A self-employed person sets aside two future payment envelopes beside last-year accounts and a calendar.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Understand your Self Assessment tax bill: Payments on account
GOV.UK — Understand your Self Assessment tax bill: Overview
GOV.UK — Self Assessment tax returns: Deadlines
GOV.UK — Pay your Self Assessment tax bill: Overview

content:
Payments on account are advance payments towards the next Self Assessment liability, normally due on 31 January and 31 July. Each is usually half the relevant previous-year bill. Your first January can include the balance for one year and an advance payment for the next.

How the two instalments work

GOV.UK explains that you can spread the cost by paying in two instalments. Each payment is usually half of the tax you owed last year. They are due by midnight on 31 January and 31 July.

On 31 January you may also owe a balancing payment for the year you have just reported, alongside the first payment on account towards the following year. That stack is why January often looks like two demands at once.

When they might not apply

According to GOV.UK, you must make the two payments unless either:

  • the tax you owed last year was less than £1,000, or
  • last year you paid more than 80% of the tax you owed outside Self Assessment (for example through your tax code, or because tax was already deducted at source on some income)

Clearer numbers (January stack)

Suppose last year’s Self Assessment bill was £4,000. Payments on account towards the next year are usually £2,000 by 31 January and £2,000 by 31 July.

If you had already paid £1,800 on account during the previous cycle against that £4,000 bill, your January amount might look like:

  • £2,200 balancing payment (£4,000 − £1,800), plus
  • £2,000 first payment on account towards the following year

So £4,200 could be due on one January date even though nothing “mysterious” has happened. If the following year’s final bill is only £3,000, the excess paid on account is typically settled through the balancing calculation. It is not lost.

Reducing payments on account

If you expect to owe less than last year, you can ask HMRC to reduce payments on account (online or by post) using a realistic estimate. Do not reduce them casually: GOV.UK is clear that if you reduce them and your bill turns out higher than expected, you can be charged interest on the difference. For the how-to steps, see how to reduce Self Assessment payments on account.

Filing dates vs this article

Filing deadlines are covered in the Self Assessment deadline guide. This page is about the advance-payment rhythm that often surprises people after a larger SA bill.

If you cannot pay

Contact HMRC early and use the payment options on GOV.UK. Late payment can attract interest and late payment penalties on unpaid tax. Filing on time still matters while you sort payment.

If you want help preparing the return that feeds these figures, TaxSimba’s Self Assessment service works from the information you provide. We do not promise a lower bill or a particular payment outcome. Always check your HMRC statement and current GOV.UK guidance.

Keep payments on account out of the earlier-year total

Illustrative preparation example.

An illustrative £4,000 relevant bill can be accompanied by a £2,000 first payment on account, making £6,000 due in January before other adjustments. The second £2,000 instalment belongs on the July line. Do not describe the £8,000 combined payments as all being tax on one year.

Check: Which payment settles the earlier year and which is an advance towards the next?

Are payments on account a separate tax?

They advance part of the next Self Assessment liability. The later return reconciles what you actually owe with amounts already paid.

Does filing early mean paying immediately?

Submitting a return early does not normally bring forward the statutory payment date. Check the dated charges on your account, particularly any older overdue amounts.

title: Late Self Assessment Filing — Penalties and What To Do Now
excerpt: Already late on Self Assessment? Here are the classic late filing and late payment penalties, how the MTD-era penalty rules differ for relevant tax years, and what to do next.
metaTitle: Late Self Assessment: Penalties and Next Steps | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Late with Self Assessment? Check which penalty rules apply, separate filing from payment and prepare evidence before contacting HMRC or appealing.
featuredImageAlt: A taxpayer opens a late-return letter and gathers records with a calm accountant; serious but reassuring, no threatening symbols.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Self Assessment tax returns: Penalties
GOV.UK — Penalties for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
GOV.UK — Self Assessment tax returns: Deadlines
GOV.UK — Pay your Self Assessment tax bill: Overview

content:
File the outstanding return, check the penalty notice and deal with unpaid tax promptly. The penalty rules depend on the tax year and whether the new MTD regime applies. No tax to pay does not automatically remove a late-filing penalty.

For dates and preparation before the deadline, use the preventive guide on Self Assessment deadlines. This page is for when you are already late, or about to be.

Which penalty regime applies?

Do not blend these two systems.

Classic Self Assessment penalties (the familiar £100 / daily / percentage-or-£300 structure) still apply to tax years that are not under the new Making Tax Digital for Income Tax penalty rules. That includes previous tax years after you join MTD. Example from GOV.UK: if you use MTD from 6 April 2026, the current (classic) penalties still apply to your 2025 to 2026 return deadline of 31 January 2027.

New MTD Income Tax penalties apply from the tax year you join Making Tax Digital for Income Tax. They replace the classic late submission and late payment penalties for your personal tax return for that year onward (with limited exceptions such as some trust, estate, partnership or non-resident company returns). See GOV.UK: Penalties for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax.

If you are unsure which year and regime you are dealing with, check your HMRC messages and the two GOV.UK pages linked in the sources. Do not assume the amounts below apply to every return forever.

Classic Self Assessment late filing penalties

Where the classic regime applies, GOV.UK sets out that if you need to send a Self Assessment tax return and you send it late, you can get:

  • an initial £100 penalty
  • after 3 months, daily penalties of £10 per day, up to a maximum of £900
  • after 6 months, a further penalty of 5% of the tax due or £300, whichever is greater
  • after 12 months, another 5% or £300 charge, whichever is greater

Partnership returns can create penalties for each partner when the partnership return is late. GOV.UK also notes a separate “failure to notify” risk if you register late after 5 October and do not pay your bill by 31 January. Check the Self Assessment penalties page for the wording that applies to you.

Classic late payment penalties

Under the classic rules, paying late can bring penalties of 5% of the unpaid tax at 30 days, 6 months and 12 months, plus interest. Filing on time but leaving the bill unpaid is still a problem.

MTD-era late submission and late payment

Once the new MTD penalties apply for a tax year, late submission uses penalty points rather than the classic £100 starting charge for that year’s return (and, after 2026 to 2027, for quarterly updates too).

In outline for people required to use MTD: the point threshold is 4; reaching it brings a £200 penalty, with further £200 charges for later missed deadlines while at the threshold. For 2026 to 2027 specifically, HMRC will not apply penalty points for late quarterly updates. Points can still apply for a late tax return for that year, and you still need to send quarterly updates before you can submit the return.

Late payment penalties under MTD are also different. They are proportionate to how long the tax stays unpaid (with a longer “first year” window), and they do not apply to payments on account. Late payment interest still applies. Full tables and conditions are on the GOV.UK MTD penalties page. This summary is not a substitute for that page.

What to do now

  1. File the outstanding return with the best complete information you can support.
  2. Pay what you can and use HMRC’s published payment routes if you need time.
  3. Read any penalty notice. Payment deadlines and appeal rights matter.
  4. Consider a reasonable excuse appeal only where it genuinely fits. “I was busy” is rarely enough on its own.
  5. Prevent a repeat with earlier document gathering, or accountant help for the next cycle.

If you need a return prepared properly rather than guessing alone, TaxSimba’s Self Assessment service works from documents you provide. An accountant prepares and reviews, and you approve before filing where that step applies. We do not guarantee penalty cancellation. Related reading: documents checklist, payments on account, and how to amend a return if the figures themselves need correcting after you file.

Match each charge to the notice

Illustrative preparation example.

You receive a late-filing penalty and a separate late-payment charge. Record the year, type, amount and issue date for each. Filing the return deals with the missing submission, while payment and any appeal need separate action.

Check: Have you checked the applicable regime and response deadline for each individual notice?

Actions to take
CheckPractical action
Which return and tax year are overdue?Identify the year and applicable penalty regime before using a penalty calculator.
Is filing, payment or both outstanding?Progress the return and the payment discussion separately; an inability to pay does not remove filing duties.
Does the notice offer an appeal route?Record its deadline and prepare a factual timeline with supporting evidence.

Will joining MTD cancel an older penalty?

No. Earlier tax years keep the rules that apply to them. Read the notice for the particular obligation rather than assuming new software resets the account.

Can I wait for an appeal decision before filing?

An appeal does not itself remove an outstanding return. Complete the required filing and follow the notice's instructions on payment while the appeal is considered.

  • Prepare a dated explanation with supporting evidence.
  • Record filing confirmation and any payment arrangement separately.

title: MTD Quarterly Deadline: What You Need to Do Before 7 November 2026
excerpt: The next Making Tax Digital quarterly update for many people in 2026 to 2027 is due by 7 November 2026. Here is what that deadline covers and what to do before it.
metaTitle: MTD Deadline 7 November 2026: Your Checklist | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Prepare the MTD update due 7 November 2026: check the cumulative period, reconcile records, send through compatible software and retain confirmation.
featuredImageAlt: A landlord prepares an autumn quarterly update, autumn leaves outside and a calendar beside reconciled records.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax - Send quarterly updates - Guidance
GOV.UK — Use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax - Using Making Tax Digital for Income Tax for the first time  - Guidance
GOV.UK — Penalties for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax

content:
Deadline in focus: if you use standard or calendar update periods for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax in 2026 to 2027, the second quarterly update is due by 7 November 2026. You can send it any time after the update period ends. You do not have to wait until the deadline day.

Update after 7 November 2026: that Making Tax Digital quarterly deadline has passed. If you still need to send the update that was due by 7 November 2026, use the missed quarterly update guide for catch-up steps. Below is what that specific deadline covered, so you can check you sent the right period.

This page is only about the 7 November 2026 quarterly deadline, not a full explainer of every MTD update. For what quarterly updates contain in general, see MTD quarterly updates explained.

Which period did the 7 November update cover?

GOV.UK sets the same send-by date for both period types:

  • Standard update periods (tax year aligned): totals from 6 April to 5 October, send by 7 November
  • Calendar update periods (1 April–31 March accounting): totals from 1 April to 30 September, send by 7 November

Each update is cumulative from the start of the tax year to the end of that period. Your software should show the exact window that applies to you.

Before 7 November: checklist

Checklist for the 7 November 2026 update

  1. Confirm you are in MTD for the income sources involved (self-employment, property, or both).
  2. Bring digital records up to date through the end of the update period (amounts, dates and categories in compatible software, or with your agent).
  3. Check joint property choices if relevant: for jointly let property, GOV.UK allows income-and-expenses or income-only in quarterly updates (expenses must be sorted later if you omit them).
  4. Send the update through compatible software, or ask your accountant/agent to send it.
  5. Diary the next dates, typically 7 February 2027 and 7 May 2027 for later 2026 to 2027 updates when periods align.

Penalties for this particular deadline

For the 2026 to 2027 tax year, HMRC will not apply penalty points for late quarterly updates. That soft landing does not make the update optional: you still need to send quarterly updates before you can submit your tax return. Late tax returns and late payment of tax can still attract penalties. Re-check GOV.UK MTD penalties for the year you are in.

If records are behind this week

Prioritise usable totals from bank exports, invoices and (for landlords) agent statements covering the period. Guessing figures just to clear a screen is a poor fix. If you want the workflow handled rather than DIY catch-up alone, TaxSimba’s Making Tax Digital service is accountant-led. You still supply the evidence.

If you still have not sent it

Follow the catch-up sequence in the missed quarterly update guide. TaxSimba’s Making Tax Digital service is accountant-led if you want help organising records. You still supply the evidence.

Confirm dates in your software and on current GOV.UK guidance.

Check the export starts at the right date

Illustrative preparation example.

You download July-to-September bank activity for the second update. That export alone does not explain the full cumulative totals. Keep the earlier records and check the software’s selected reporting basis before approving the update.

Check: Does the proposed submission reconcile to the entire cumulative coverage period?

Actions to take
CheckPractical action
Standard or calendar periods?Confirm the actual cumulative window shown in software before reconciling totals.
Are all relevant businesses covered?Check each required business update and any earlier missing submission.
Has HMRC accepted the update?Save the dated acknowledgement and period; a completed upload to your accountant alone is not submission evidence.

Do I have to wait until 7 November?

No. Send after the relevant period ends once your records are ready. Allow time to resolve access, record or software problems.

What if the deadline has already passed?

Check the missing obligation in software and send the required update promptly. The 2026/27 quarterly penalty concession does not make updates optional or cover every other tax obligation.

  • Assign a named sender and an earlier internal deadline.
  • Save acknowledgement, period and any follow-up action.

title: MTD for Landlords: What Landlords Need to Do in 2026/27
excerpt: If Making Tax Digital for Income Tax applies to your property income in 2026 to 2027, here is what landlords actually need to do — digital records, quarterly updates, and joint-let points.
metaTitle: MTD for Landlords 2026/27: Records and Updates | TaxSimba
metaDescription: Check MTD for landlords in 2026/27: qualifying income, joint-property shares, digital rental records, quarterly updates and year-end preparation.
featuredImageAlt: A landlord reviews several UK rental statements with a small house model and a green folder.

sources.label: GOV.UK — Use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax - Create digital records - Guidance
GOV.UK — Use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax - Send quarterly updates - Guidance
GOV.UK — Find out if and when you need to use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
GOV.UK — Work out your qualifying income for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax

content:
Landlords in MTD keep digital property records and send cumulative updates, then complete the annual return. Check your own share of qualifying income, any other trades and the correct lookback year. One jointly owned property does not automatically mean both owners have identical obligations.

This guide is about the landlord obligations themselves. If you already know you need managed help, the commercial service page is MTD for landlords.

Does MTD apply to your property income?

MTD for Income Tax can apply if you are on Self Assessment with property income (alone or with a trade) and your qualifying income (gross self-employment and property turnover before expenses) sits above the look-back threshold. The April 2026 wave used more than £50,000 on the 2024 to 2025 return; later waves use £30,000 (from April 2027) and £20,000 (from April 2028). Check GOV.UK or the MTD checker. Do not use profit after mortgage interest as the test.

For jointly owned property, only your share of the relevant property income counts toward that qualifying-income total. GOV.UK’s example style: a property generating £50,000 of income owned equally with one other person gives you £25,000 toward your threshold (before adding any self-employment turnover).

What landlords must keep digitally

GOV.UK expects digital records of UK property income (rent, certain premiums/inducements) and property expenses (repairs, maintenance, and other allowable categories your software supports). You still keep supporting documents such as agent statements and invoices.

Useful nuance: UK rental properties are generally treated as one UK property business. You do not create a separate MTD “set” for each flat in the UK. The software rolls them together (including your share of jointly let UK property). Foreign property has separate record rules; check GOV.UK if you have overseas lets.

Example entry: rent received £1,250 on 1 September 2026, categorised as property income; a boiler repair of £240 on 12 June 2026 as repairs and maintenance. The agent statement and invoice stay on file.

Quarterly updates for property

Every three months, software totals those digital records and sends category summaries. HMRC does not receive every individual receipt. Deadlines for many people in 2026 to 2027 include 7 August, 7 November, 7 February and 7 May (following tax year). Details: what quarterly updates include.

For jointly let property, GOV.UK lets you include income and expenses, or income only, in quarterly updates. If you omit expenses you must report them later by resending the fourth update before the tax return.

Landlord-specific traps

  • Treating profit after mortgage interest as the MTD threshold test
  • Counting a joint property’s full rent toward your threshold instead of your share
  • Leaving agent statements in an email inbox until January
  • Mixing personal and rental spending with no labels
  • Assuming “I only have two buy-to-lets” means two separate UK MTD property businesses (usually it does not)

TaxSimba is an accountant-led MTD service, not DIY landlord software. For product and packages aimed at landlords, start at rental income / MTD for landlords. Rules and exemptions can change; confirm on GOV.UK for your situation.

Reconcile properties before combining the business

Illustrative preparation example.

One letting agent manages two UK flats and another manages a third. Reconcile each statement to the underlying rent, fees and ownership share before combining the relevant property-business totals. A payout from one agent is not the whole portfolio.

Check: Are all properties, ownership shares and agent deductions represented once?

Actions to take
CheckPractical action
Is your qualifying-income total correct?Use the relevant gross trading and property figures, including your share of joint income.
Do agent statements match the bank?Bridge gross rent, fees and net payouts rather than treating the bank credit as the whole record.
Do you also have overseas property?Identify it separately so the appropriate property business and reporting rules are checked.

Does each UK flat need its own quarterly update?

UK properties are normally combined within one UK property business. Keep the underlying property records so totals and ownership shares can still be explained.

Do mortgage repayments reduce the MTD threshold?

No. The qualifying-income test uses gross income before expenses. Residential finance-cost relief is a separate year-end tax question.

  • Total gross rent for the relevant look-back year.
  • Reconcile each agent's gross-to-net statements.
  • Separate UK and overseas property records.
  • Confirm who sends updates and prepares the annual return.

excerpt: Sole traders in Making Tax Digital for Income Tax in 2026 to 2027 need digital business records and quarterly updates. Here is the practical checklist — without the sales brochure.
metaTitle: MTD for Sole Traders 2026/27: Practical Guide | TaxSimba

content:
Sole traders in MTD need digital business records, quarterly updates and an annual return through compatible software. Use gross qualifying income and the correct lookback year to check the start date. Keep the reporting dates separate from the tax payment schedule.

Looking for the managed service rather than the rules? That commercial page is MTD for sole traders.

When a sole trader is in scope

You need MTD when you are Self Assessment-registered with self-employment income (and sometimes property too) and your qualifying income (turnover before expenses) clears the look-back threshold. From 6 April 2026 that meant more than £50,000 on the 2024 to 2025 return; from 6 April 2027 it is more than £30,000 on 2025 to 2026; from 6 April 2028 it is more than £20,000 on 2026 to 2027. Profit after costs is the wrong figure for this test. Use GOV.UK or the MTD checker if you are unsure.

Digital records for a trade

Record sales, fees and allowable expenses with amount, date and category in software that works with MTD. Supporting invoices and bank exports still matter. If you run more than one sole-trader business, GOV.UK expects separate digital records, and separate quarterly updates, for each (for example electrician work and a separate tutoring trade).

Example: a freelance designer invoices a client £1,800 on 14 September 2026 (category: turnover/sales) and pays £45 for design software on 3 September 2026 (category: office costs, or the nearest match your software uses). Both sit in the digital records with the invoice and receipt kept as evidence, not reconstructed from a vague bank line in January.

More on the record trail: MTD digital records.

Quarterly rhythm without the jargon

Software totals your digital records into category summaries every three months. Those summaries are not full tax returns, and HMRC does not see every receipt. Typical deadlines when periods align include 7 August, 7 November, 7 February and 7 May. For 2026 to 2027, late quarterly updates do not attract penalty points, but updates are still required before the return can be submitted.

Sole trader checklist for 2026/27

  1. Confirm scope (threshold + Self Assessment status).
  2. Authorise compatible software or an agent.
  3. Keep digital records from the start of the relevant tax year (catch up if you joined late).
  4. Send each quarterly update on time for every trade in MTD.
  5. At year-end, use the software route to adjustments, other income, reliefs and the tax return.

If you want accountant-led MTD support rather than DIY-only software, compare the offering on the sole trader MTD page. Always check current GOV.UK guidance for your trades.

Give a personal transfer a different label

Illustrative preparation example.

Your sole-trade account receives £700 from a customer and £500 from your savings. Keep the £500 transfer identifiable so it is not counted as another sale. Support the customer payment with the sales record and check any cash receipts separately.

Check: Can you explain every receipt without assuming that every deposit is turnover?

Any cash or platform receipts outside the feed?Bring them into the records and reconcile them without duplicating bank transfers.
Who handles year-end work?Confirm adjustments, other income and the annual return as well as quarterly submissions.

Does the threshold use profit after expenses?

No. Qualifying income starts from gross self-employment and property income for the relevant look-back year. Costs and tax reliefs are separate calculations.

Can an accountant run the software process?

Yes, with appropriate authorisation and an agreed scope. You still need to supply complete source records and review questions about the figures.
